stem: Your contract pipeline flags high-risk clauses for legal review using the rule "flag a clause only when it exposes the company to more than one million dollars of liability". The model receives the contract text and nothing else: no claim history, no exposure model, no revenue figures. It flags 31% of clauses, including a standard mutual confidentiality clause, and last month it passed over an uncapped indemnity. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Trigger on features the clause text shows: an uncapped indemnity, a unilateral termination right, or a liability cap left blank.
Have the model estimate the dollar exposure of each clause and flag every clause whose own estimate is above one million.
Give the model the finance team's exposure model and last year's claim history so it can apply the existing dollar threshold.
Keep the rule and add a second pass that re-reads each flagged clause and drops the ones it judges to be low risk after all.

explanation: A criterion has to be evaluable from what the model is actually given. Dollar exposure appears nowhere in the contract text, so the threshold collapses into a guess. Naming the clause features that signal risk makes the judgement observable in the same document the model already reads.

why.B: The estimate is a figure the model invents from text containing no exposure data, so the threshold is applied to a fabricated number.
why.C: Builds a data pipeline to preserve a threshold no clause states, when the observable clause features already separate the two cases.
why.D: Adds a pass that re-applies the same unevaluable rule, so it inherits the criterion that produced the false positives.

stem: Your review bot reports functions that are too complex to maintain, using the rule "flag any function longer than 60 lines". Developers dismiss 84% of those findings and most hits are generated serializers and long but flat configuration builders. In the same month the bot said nothing about a 34-line payment router with nine nested conditionals that later caused an outage. What should you change?

options.text: Raise the line threshold to 120 so the flat generated files stop matching, and leave the rule unchanged otherwise.
Remove the complexity category, since maintainability is a judgement a review bot should not be making about a codebase.
Flag on the property that matters: branch count and nesting depth inside a function, not the lines it happens to occupy.
Have the bot rate each function's maintainability from 1 to 10 and report only the functions it puts in the bottom band.

explanation: The criterion is explicit and still wrong, because it names a proxy rather than the property the team cares about. Line count tracks complexity poorly, while branch count and nesting are visible in the same source the bot already reads and separate the generated serializers from the payment router.

why.A: Moves a threshold on the wrong property, so flat generated code still matches at some length and the nine-branch router still does not.
why.B: Drops a category the outage shows is needed, when the defect is a fixable criterion rather than an unmeasurable one.
why.D: Replaces a measurable rule with an unanchored self-assigned score, which is the vague judgement problem in numeric form.

stem: Your research synthesis prompt carries two inclusion rules: "include a finding only when the paper reports an effect size" and "always include findings that change clinical guidance". On papers that change guidance but report no effect size, the agent included the finding in 3 of last month's reports and dropped it in 5. Reviewers cannot tell which reports are complete. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add two to four examples of papers that change guidance without an effect size, each showing the inclusion decision and why.
State which rule wins where both apply, and have the report mark such a finding as included with no effect size reported.
Tell the agent to use its judgement when the two rules disagree, since these papers are rare and each one differs a little.
Have a reviewer decide inclusion for every paper the agent identifies as matching one rule but not the other.

explanation: The two rules are each explicit but they collide, and nothing in the prompt says which one governs the overlap. Naming the precedence removes the inconsistency, and marking the finding keeps the report honest about why it is there without an effect size.

why.A: Examples cannot settle a contradiction the prompt still states both ways, and any paper unlike the examples stays ambiguous.
why.C: Names the collision and hands it back to the judgement that has already produced two different answers on the same case.
why.D: Moves a decision the prompt can make once onto a person for every report, and the rules stay contradictory underneath.

stem: Your invoice prompt carries 14 few-shot examples. Two of them cover a shipping charge listed among the line items: one puts it in line_items and excludes it from the subtotal, the other counts it toward the subtotal. Shipping is handled one way on roughly half of invoices and the other way on the rest, and adding a fifteenth example showing the intended handling did not settle it. What is the problem?

options.text: Fourteen examples are more than the model can hold at once, so the ones nearest the start lose their influence.
The examples belong in the extraction tool's schema description rather than the prompt, where they compete with the instructions.
Two examples demonstrate opposite handling of the same case, so the example set is itself the source of the inconsistency.
The examples show the output but never the reasoning, so the model cannot work out which treatment a new invoice needs.

explanation: Few-shot examples are a strong signal, and two examples that handle one case in opposite ways teach the disagreement rather than resolve it. A fifteenth example leaves the contradiction in place; the fix is to correct or remove whichever of the two is wrong.

why.A: Capacity is not the constraint, since the other twelve examples produce consistent behaviour on the cases they cover.
why.B: Relocating the examples carries the contradiction with them, and a schema description is not where worked examples belong.
why.D: Shown reasoning helps on a genuinely ambiguous case, but here the prompt states both answers for one identical case.

stem: Your CI review bot posts findings as inline comments and must comment only on lines the pull request changed. About 9% of its comments land on untouched lines in files it read for context, where the platform displays them at the top of the file and developers read them as noise. A teammate proposes adding few-shot examples showing findings that stay inside the diff. How should you respond?

options.text: Agree: few-shot examples are the most effective technique for making output consistent, and this is an output consistency problem.
Expand the prompt with a firmer statement that only changed lines may be commented on, and measure the rate again after a week.
Give the bot the diff alone with no surrounding file content, so lines outside the change are not available for it to comment on.
Filter out findings whose file and line fall outside the changed hunks before posting, since the rule is absolute and belongs in code.

explanation: The rule holds on every comment or not at all, and few-shot examples shape likelihood rather than guarantee behaviour. A deterministic filter over the changed hunks is the smallest change that enforces it.

why.A: Few-shot raises compliance but cannot guarantee a rule that has to hold on every comment the bot posts.
why.B: Prompt wording has the same probabilistic limit and gives the bot no new information about where the hunks end.
why.C: Removes the surrounding context that makes the findings accurate, trading a posting defect for worse review quality.

stem: Your review prompt carries six few-shot examples of resource leaks, each showing a file handle opened and never closed together with the finding to post. The bot now catches those reliably, but it also posts a leak finding on handles closed in a with block or a try/finally, and developers dismiss 6 of every 10 leak findings. What should you add?

options.text: Contrasting examples of handles that are correctly released, each stating why no finding was posted for that code.
Six further examples of genuine leaks, taken from the modules where this month's dismissed findings were posted.
A prompt line saying not to report a leak when the handle is closed anywhere inside the enclosing function body.
A post-filter that drops a leak finding whenever the flagged line sits inside a with block or a try/finally.

explanation: Examples that all show the finding teach what to report and nothing about what to leave alone, so lookalike code matches. A few contrasting examples with the reason attached let the model separate an accepted pattern from a genuine issue and carry that distinction to constructs the examples never name.

why.B: More of the positive case sharpens a signal the bot already follows and says nothing about what a non-leak looks like.
why.C: One stated exception covers the two constructs seen so far and misses the next one, where paired examples teach the distinction itself.
why.D: Encodes the same two exceptions in code and discards genuine findings where a handle is released on only one path.

stem: Your review bot returns findings through a tool schema in which file, line, issue, severity and suggested_fix are all required strings. On findings about a design problem, for example a module that should be split, suggested_fix holds a one-line edit that does not compile and does not address the finding. On typo findings the fix is correct and useful. What is the correct change?

options.text: Keep suggested_fix required and validate that its text parses in the file's language before the finding is posted.
Make suggested_fix nullable and state in the prompt that null is correct when no single edit resolves the finding.
Keep suggested_fix required and add "write 'no automated fix available' when no concrete fix exists" to the prompt.
Split the schema into two tools, one for findings that carry a code fix and one for design findings that do not.

explanation: A required field pressures the model to produce something for every finding, including findings where no single edit exists. Making the field nullable removes that pressure, which is the smallest change that stops the fabrication.

why.A: Rejects fabricated fixes that fail to parse and keeps the ones that parse and are still wrong, and the field stays required.
why.C: Leaves the field required and turns a sentinel string into a prompt convention every downstream consumer has to special-case.
why.D: Adds a second schema and a tool choice to solve what one optional field solves, and the model can pick the wrong tool.

stem: payment_status is an enum with paid, unpaid and partial, and it decides whether an account goes to collections. Statements with no payment section at all already return null and route to a separate queue. On statements where the section is present but unresolvable, for example "balance carried forward, see attached remittance", the model returns unpaid. Collections chased 300 customers last quarter who had in fact paid. What is the correct schema change?

options.text: Add unclear to the enum with a detail string for the wording that made it unclear, and route unclear to review.
Return null for these statements as well, so one value covers both a missing payment section and an unresolvable one.
Keep the enum and add "when the status cannot be determined, choose the option that is safest for the business" to the prompt.
Return payment_status as free text so the document's own wording survives into the pipeline and can be interpreted there.

explanation: The model has no value for a case it cannot resolve, so it is forced into a definite one. An unclear member with a detail string makes the ambiguity representable and routable instead of collapsing it into unpaid.

why.B: Merges two cases that need different handling into one value, so the queue for statements with no payment section cannot tell them apart.
why.C: Still forces an unresolvable case into a definite value, and "safest for the business" is a judgement the prompt leaves undefined.
why.D: Removes the constrained vocabulary that collections routing depends on and moves the classification into a downstream parser.

stem: After the model fabricated purchase order numbers, your team made every field in the invoice schema nullable. The fabrication stopped. Reconciliation now shows 22% of records arriving with a null invoice_number, invoice_date or total, all fields printed on every invoice in the corpus, and those records pass validation and load into the ledger unnoticed. What is the correct schema change?

options.text: Add a found_in_document boolean beside every field so the loader can tell a genuine absence from a value the model missed.
Restore required on the fields every invoice carries, leaving nullable only where the source may genuinely omit the value.
Keep every field nullable and add a prompt line saying null is correct only when the value is truly absent from the document.
Keep the schema and have the loader reject any record holding a null in one of the three fields, then queue it for re-extraction.

explanation: Nullable belongs on fields the source may legitimately omit, not on every field. Making the always-present fields required again turns a missed extraction into a validation failure the retry loop can act on, while the genuinely optional fields keep the nullability that stopped the fabrication.

why.A: Duplicates in a second field what required already expresses, and the boolean is as fabricable as the value it describes.
why.C: Leaves nothing enforcing the distinction, so a missed value still validates and still reaches the ledger unnoticed.
why.D: Catches three named fields after the fact in a component that cannot see the document, and every new field needs its own loader rule.

stem: Your CI step runs claude -p with a prompt ending "reply with a JSON array of findings", and a shell script strips code fences and takes the longest bracketed span before parsing. About 5% of runs still fail to parse. Last month you made the script exit non-zero on a parse failure, so the team now loses roughly one build a day to output that is not a code problem. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Keep hardening the salvage heuristics in the script, since each new preamble the model produces can be handled once it is seen.
Move the step into a Claude Code skill so the output format rules live in SKILL.md rather than in the shell command.
Run the step with --output-format json and pass the finding schema with --json-schema, then read the structured result.
Add "return only the raw JSON array, with no preamble and no code fence" to the prompt and keep the existing parser.

explanation: The CLI can return a result constrained by a schema, which removes the free-text response the script is trying to salvage. No amount of parser repair makes an unconstrained response reliable, because the next wrapper is one the heuristics have not met yet.

why.A: Chases each new wrapper only after it has broken a build, and the response stays free text the script has to guess at.
why.B: Puts the same prose instruction in a different file and leaves the output itself entirely unconstrained.
why.D: Relies on prompt compliance where the CLI can enforce a schema, and the parser still has to guess when compliance slips.

stem: Your extraction retry loop resends the paper, the failed extraction and the exact validation error, capped at two attempts, and it clears 88% of failures. Nothing about a failure is recorded beyond a counter, so nobody can say which schema rule keeps firing, and the documents that exhaust both attempts land in one dead-letter table holding only the raw PDF. Which two changes should you make? (Select 2)

options.text: Record the failing field and constraint on every attempt, so recurring failures group by rule and point at the prompt line to fix.
Raise the cap to five attempts, since the third and later attempts would clear part of the residual the loop currently gives up on.
Split the dead-letter outcome by cause, separating a value the paper does not contain from an extraction the model got wrong.
Have a second model read each dead-letter document and write the extraction the first attempt should have produced.

explanation: A retry loop that records only a counter cannot improve the prompt that causes the retries. Attributing each failure to the field and constraint that fired makes the recurring class visible, and separating the dead letters by cause keeps papers that genuinely omit a value out of a queue meant for extraction defects.

why.B: Adds attempts with no evidence they clear anything, and every failure stays as unattributed as it is today.
why.D: Adds a model to compensate for a loop nobody can diagnose, and its output faces none of the validation the first attempt failed.

stem: Your review bot returns findings through a validated schema, and it receives the full file and the diff on every run. Every finding is about a specific changed line. To stop a retry loop that would not settle, a developer changed the retry to drop whichever field failed validation and resubmit, and validation failures went to zero. Reconciliation now shows 14% of posted findings carry no line number, and the platform displays those at the top of the file. What is the right design?

options.text: Restore the field, keep the retry capped, and hold a finding that still fails validation rather than posting it stripped.
Make line optional in the schema, which matches what the pipeline already does and lets the posted findings validate honestly.
Keep dropping the field that failed but record which field was dropped, so the rate of stripped findings can be tracked.
Retry the stripped findings once more with the file contents attached, so the model can supply the line number it left out.

explanation: Dropping the field that fails validation makes the validator agree with itself and destroys the guarantee it existed to provide. The constraint should stand, and a finding that still cannot meet it should be held back rather than published without the field its consumer requires.

why.B: Every finding names a specific changed line, so an optional line codifies the defect rather than a legitimate absence.
why.C: Measures the damage without stopping it, and the stripped findings keep reaching the pull request as noise.
why.D: The full file is already in the request, so a further attempt has nothing new, and the loop still publishes what fails.

stem: Every finding your bot posts carries detected_pattern, the code construct that triggered it. This month's dismissals group cleanly: builder_method_returns_this is 38% of all dismissals at a 97% dismissal rate, while every other pattern sits below 20%. Correctness findings overall are accepted 79% of the time. What should you do with this?

options.text: Disable the correctness category until its overall dismissal rate falls below 10%, then reinstate it with the same criteria.
Write an explicit exclusion for that construct, with an example of a fluent builder and of a real dropped return value.
Raise the bar so a correctness finding is posted only when the bot is highly confident the return value matters.
Ask developers to add a suppression comment above each builder method so the bot skips those call sites.

explanation: The feedback loop has already isolated one construct inside an otherwise trusted category, so the proportionate fix is to correct the criteria for that construct and leave the rest of the category running.

why.A: Removes a category accepted 79% of the time to deal with one construct inside it, and brings it back unchanged.
why.C: A confidence qualifier does not encode the difference between a fluent builder and a dropped result, which is the distinction being missed.
why.D: Puts maintenance on every developer for a rule the prompt can state once.

stem: A monthly compliance summary of merged pull requests is due on the 5th at 17:00. The source data is complete on the 3rd at 09:00. The work has two dependent stages: stage 1 extracts the change facts per pull request, and stage 2 summarises stage 1's output and cannot start until stage 1 returns. Retrieval and publishing take 2 hours after stage 2. Planning against the documented worst case of 24 hours per batch, and taking the 50% saving wherever the deadline allows it, which plan should you use?

options.text: Run both stages synchronously, since a stage that depends on the previous stage's output rules out the batch API.
Submit both stages as a single batch request and let stage 2 consume stage 1's output inside that same request.
Run stage 1 on the batch API submitted on the 4th at 09:00 and stage 2 synchronously, since two batch windows will not fit.
Run stage 1 on the batch API submitted on the 3rd at 09:00 and stage 2 on the batch API as soon as stage 1 returns.

explanation: There are 56 hours between the 3rd at 09:00 and the deadline. Two worst-case 24-hour windows plus 2 hours of publishing is 50 hours, so both stages fit on the batch API with 6 hours to spare.

why.A: Pays full price for a workload with 56 hours of slack, on a premise the arithmetic does not support.
why.B: A batch request cannot take an intermediate result mid-request, so it cannot chain a dependent second stage.
why.C: Two 24-hour windows plus publishing is 50 hours and fits inside the 56 available, so stage 2 gives up half its saving for nothing.

stem: Your team runs four Claude workloads and wants to move whatever fits onto the Message Batches API for the 50% saving, planning against the documented worst case of 24 hours per batch. Which two workloads belong on it? (Select 2)

options.text: The pre-merge review that blocks a merge until its findings are posted, which runs about 90 times a day across the team.
Nightly test generation over the day's merged commits, with the suggestions opened as draft pull requests the next morning.
The failure explainer a developer runs from the terminal while a red build waits, which summarises the failing test for them.
The monthly compliance report over the quarter's merged pull requests, assembled from data that is complete on the first.

explanation: Batch fits work that nothing is waiting on and where a full day of processing still lands inside the deadline. The nightly generation and the monthly report both have that slack, and both are read long after the window closes.

why.A: A merge waits on the result, so a run that may take a day turns a pre-merge gate into a blocking delay.
why.C: A developer is sitting in front of a red build, so a latency-tolerant queue is the wrong place for the request.

stem: You are about to submit 40,000 contracts as one batch run. The extraction schema gained three fields last week and the prompt was updated for them, but nothing has been run against the new prompt yet. If the prompt is wrong you find out when results return, up to 24 hours later, and the run has to be redone. What should you do first?

options.text: Submit the full run and use custom_id to identify and resubmit whatever comes back failing validation.
Split the 40,000 into ten batches submitted an hour apart, so a defect shows up in the first batch before the rest complete.
Run about 50 contracts through the synchronous API, fix what fails validation, then submit the full batch.
Submit the full run and add a validation-retry loop that corrects failed extractions as the results are read back.

explanation: The failure mode here applies to every request rather than to individual documents, and batch turnaround makes discovering it expensive. A small synchronous sample surfaces a prompt defect in minutes, so the large run is submitted once.

why.A: A prompt defect fails most of the 40,000, so the resubmission is the whole run again and another day of delay.
why.B: Each batch completes on its own schedule inside the same window, so the tenth may go in before the first has returned.
why.D: A retry loop corrects individual extractions and cannot repair a prompt that is wrong for every document in the run.

stem: Your extraction pipeline adds a separate verification pass that re-reads the document alongside the record and returns a confidence for each field. You now have to decide what the pipeline does with those numbers. Which two designs use the signal soundly? (Select 2)

options.text: Route any field whose confidence falls below a set threshold to human review and let the rest load unattended.
Auto-approve every field above 0.9 and retire the human review step, since the verification pass has already checked those.
Set the threshold from a labelled sample, comparing each confidence band against the field accuracy measured within it.
Have the extraction pass report the confidence itself, which saves the second call and rates fields as they are produced.

explanation: A self-reported confidence is useful for routing and useless as a guarantee. Routing the uncertain fields to people concentrates review where it pays, and a threshold means nothing until the bands behind it have been checked against labelled data.

why.B: Retires review on the strength of an unmeasured number, so a band that is only 80% accurate is treated as certainty.
why.D: A confidence produced in the same pass as the value rates reasoning the model has already committed to, which is the self-review limitation.

stem: A 140-page master services agreement is extracted in one pass. Obligations from sections 3 to 9 come back detailed, sections 20 to 34 come back thin or missing entirely, and the defined term "Business Day" is applied correctly in one clause and ignored in another two sections later. What extraction architecture fixes this?

options.text: Send the whole agreement to a model with a larger context window so that every section gets equal attention within one pass.
Ask the counterparty for the agreement split into one file per article before the extraction pipeline runs on it.
Instruct the model to give every article equal attention and to state the section number beside each obligation it returns.
Extract section by section, then run a separate pass over defined terms and the clauses that cross-reference each other.

explanation: One pass over 140 pages dilutes attention, which is why the late sections come back thin. Per-section passes give each part consistent depth, and a separate cross-reference pass catches the consistency problems that only appear between sections.

why.A: A larger window does not fix attention dilution, which is a quality problem rather than a capacity problem.
why.B: Shifts the work outside the system and still leaves the cross-clause consistency problem unaddressed.
why.C: A prose instruction cannot restore attention across 140 pages, and a section number labels the gap without closing it.
